title: Nikhil Gupta Sentenced to 235 Months in US Prison for Pannun Murder-for-Hire Plot
excerpt: A Manhattan federal judge handed the 55-year-old Indian national 19 years and seven months on Friday, at the bottom of a guidelines range prosecutors had asked to top out at 293 months.
body:
• Nikhil Gupta, 55, was sentenced on Friday to 235 months in federal prison in Manhattan for plotting to kill Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.
  • Gupta pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering; the plot collapsed because the man he dealt with was working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration.
  • Prosecutors had asked for the maximum 293 months. The sentence sits at the bottom of the 235-to-293-month federal guidelines range.
  • Co-defendant Vikash Yadav, identified by US prosecutors as an Indian government employee, is also charged but is not in US custody. India has dissociated itself from the plot.

An Indian man who admitted orchestrating a plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City was sentenced on Friday to 235 months in prison — 19 years and seven months — by US District Judge Victor Marrero in Manhattan federal court, according to Reuters. Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

The target was Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer with Sikhs for Justice in New York, who advocates a sovereign Sikh state in northern India. Pannun was present in court for the sentencing.

How the plot unfolded

According to court records, Gupta worked in 2023 with co-defendant Vikash Yadav, identified by US prosecutors as an Indian government employee, to arrange Pannun's killing. Acting on Yadav's instructions, Gupta contacted a man he believed could supply a hitman; that man was a confidential source for the US Drug Enforcement Administration. Gupta brokered a $100,000 deal for the killing, and an associate delivered $15,000 in cash in New York in June 2023 as an advance payment to a purported hitman who was in fact an undercover US law enforcement officer.

The case became public alongside Canadian allegations of plots against Sikh separatists there, and the disclosures tested relations between India and both countries. India's government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying such action would be against government policy, and India has denied involvement in such plots.

A sentence at the bottom of the range

The 235-month term sits at the lower end of the federal sentencing guidelines range of 235 to 293 months. The US government had pushed for the maximum 293-month sentence — the term prosecutors set out before Friday's hearing — with the US Attorney's office describing Gupta's conduct in a court submission as “as brutal as it was brazen.” In court, prosecutor Ashley Nicolas told the judge the case went to the heart of the right to speak without fear of violence.

"This case cuts to the very core of American values. We don't condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever."

— Ashley Nicolas, federal prosecutor

Gupta's lawyers had sought 144 months followed by three years of supervised release, in line with a Probation Department recommendation, arguing that the punishment should reflect his clean criminal record, his age and the untreated alcohol dependence he was dealing with at the time of the offence. In a letter to the judge before sentencing, Gupta wrote that he wished he could “turn back time to 2023 and undo my mistakes,” and in court he apologised to Pannun, to the communities he hurt and to his own family, saying he regretted straying from the nonviolent example of Mahatma Gandhi.

Pannun told the court he was grateful to the United States for prosecuting Gupta and that he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty. “Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

What remains open

Yadav, the alleged Indian government handler, remains charged in the case and is not in US custody; it is unclear whether he has hired a defence lawyer. Separately, a US court has allowed Pannun to serve summons in his civil lawsuit through the Delhi courts on India's national security adviser and a former intelligence chief — a case India has called a malicious agenda. Friday's sentence closes the criminal case against Gupta himself, three years after the cash handover that exposed the plot.
